title: Radians to Degrees Converter: Angles for Humans
description: Convert radians to degrees with the Radians to Degrees Converter — the exact 180/pi factor, full precision, sign preserved. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 0.7114 radians — Times Square's latitude in the language of code — converts to 40.76 degrees, the language of humans and charts.
quick_answer: The Radians to Degrees Converter converts angles from radians to degrees by the exact factor 180 divided by pi. Enter the radians and read the degrees — the return trip from mathematics' native angle unit to the one charts and people use, at full precision.

body.t: A bearing that prints as 0.7854 is 45 degrees wearing code dress. Convert outputs while debugging — the forward lane is
Technical literature lives in radians; intuition lives in degrees. Converting the paper's worked example verifies you read the formula right.
Angular velocities, phases and oscillation answers emerge in radians per second — degrees per second is the version you can picture.
Catalogues and libraries hand angles in radians more often than amateurs expect. Convert before the telescope session, not during it.
π ≈ 3.14159 rad = 180°; π/2 = 90°; π/4 = 45°; 1 rad = 57.2958° — the odd-looking constant that is just 180/π being itself.
−1.2913 rad = −73.99° (a west longitude's angle). And 7.0 rad = 401.07° — more than a revolution; normalising to 41.07° is your choice, never the converter's silent edit.

faq: They convert with their sign — a negative angle is a direction convention (clockwise, west, south), and the converter preserves it faithfully.
They convert as given (7 rad → 401.07°). Wrapping to a single revolution is an application decision the converter leaves to you.
180/π at full double precision — conversion error is not a thing that exists at this scale; wrong-unit input is the only real hazard.
This lane is radians↔degrees, the pair the world runs on. Gradians (400 per circle) convert by 0.9 degrees each, for the surveying antiques that need them.
My code's bearing looks wrong after conversion.
Check the convention: mathematical angles grow counter-clockwise from east; bearings grow clockwise from north. The unit conversion is innocent — the reference direction is the culprit.
Below ~0.1 rad, degrees ≈ radians × 57.3 and the angle ≈ its sine — the approximation astronomers and engineers lean on daily.
